title: CHM 101 — General Chemistry I
topic: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table & Chemical Bonding
overview: This study pack covers the foundational chemistry concepts for engineering students: atomic structure, periodic trends, chemical bonding, and stoichiometry. These concepts underpin later materials science and engineering chemistry courses.

modules.title: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table
modules.summary:
Atoms are composed of protons, neutrons, and electrons, with electrons arranged in energy levels (shells) around the nucleus. The arrangement of electrons, particularly in the outermost shell, determines how an atom behaves chemically.

The periodic table organizes elements by increasing atomic number, and elements in the same column (group) share similar chemical properties because they have the same number of valence (outermost) electrons. Moving across a period, atomic radius decreases and ionization energy generally increases as nuclear charge increases.

Understanding these trends allows prediction of how elements will react and bond with each other, which is the foundation for all of chemistry.
keyPoints: Atoms consist of protons (positive), neutrons (neutral), and electrons (negative)
Electron configuration determines chemical behavior, especially valence electrons
Elements in the same periodic table group share similar chemical properties
Atomic radius decreases and ionization energy increases across a period (left to right)
Atomic number = number of protons; mass number = protons + neutrons

definitions.definition: The number of protons in an atom's nucleus, which defines the element.
Electrons in the outermost shell of an atom, responsible for chemical bonding behavior.
The energy required to remove an electron from a gaseous atom or ion.
Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
A horizontal row in the periodic table, representing elements with the same number of electron shells.

workedExamples.title: Determining Number of Subatomic Particles
workedExamples.problem: An atom of Chlorine has an atomic number of 17 and a mass number of 35. Determine the number of protons, neutrons, and electrons.

workedExamples.title: Predicting Periodic Trend
workedExamples.problem: Between Sodium (Na, atomic number 11) and Chlorine (Cl, atomic number 17), which has the larger atomic radius?
steps: Both elements are in Period 3 of the periodic table
Atomic radius decreases as you move left to right across a period due to increasing nuclear charge pulling electrons closer
Sodium is further left than Chlorine in the same period
workedExamples.answer: Sodium has the larger atomic radius.

quiz.question: What determines an atom's chemical behavior most directly?
quiz.explanation: Valence electrons, found in the outermost shell, determine how an atom bonds and reacts with others.

quiz.question: How does atomic radius change across a period (left to right)?
quiz.explanation: Atomic radius decreases across a period because increasing nuclear charge pulls electrons closer to the nucleus.

modules.title: Chemical Bonding
modules.summary:
Chemical bonds form when atoms interact to achieve a more stable electron configuration, typically by gaining, losing, or sharing electrons. The three main types of bonding are ionic, covalent, and metallic.

Ionic bonds form between a metal and a non-metal, where electrons are transferred from one atom to another, creating oppositely charged ions that attract each other. Covalent bonds form between non-metals, where atoms share electron pairs. Metallic bonding occurs in metals, where electrons are delocalized across a lattice of metal cations.

The type of bonding present in a substance directly determines its physical properties — melting point, conductivity, and solubility all trace back to bonding type, which is directly relevant to engineering material selection.
keyPoints: Ionic bonds: electron transfer between metal and non-metal, forming charged ions
Covalent bonds: electron sharing between non-metal atoms
Metallic bonds: delocalized electrons shared across a lattice of metal cations
Bonding type determines melting point, electrical conductivity, and solubility
Electronegativity difference between atoms helps predict bond type

definitions.definition: A chemical bond formed by the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, typically between a metal and non-metal.
A chemical bond formed when two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.
A bond in which electrons are delocalized and shared across a lattice of metal cations.
A measure of an atom's ability to attract shared electrons in a chemical bond.
A regular, repeating three-dimensional arrangement of atoms or ions in a solid.

workedExamples.title: Predicting Bond Type
workedExamples.problem: Determine the type of bond formed between Sodium (Na) and Chlorine (Cl) in NaCl.
steps: Sodium is a metal (Group 1), Chlorine is a non-metal (Group 17)
Metal + non-metal combinations typically form ionic bonds
Sodium loses one electron to become Na⁺; Chlorine gains that electron to become Cl⁻
The oppositely charged ions attract electrostatically
workedExamples.answer: NaCl forms an ionic bond, with Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions held together by electrostatic attraction.

workedExamples.title: Explaining Conductivity Differences
workedExamples.problem: Explain why metals conduct electricity well, but ionic solids (like NaCl) do not conduct electricity in solid form.
steps: In metals, delocalized electrons are free to move throughout the lattice, carrying electric current
In ionic solids, ions are held in fixed positions within a rigid lattice structure
Since ions cannot move freely in the solid state, no charge carriers are available to conduct current
Ionic solids only conduct electricity when melted or dissolved in water, where ions become mobile
workedExamples.answer: Metals conduct due to freely moving delocalized electrons; solid ionic compounds don't conduct because their ions are fixed in place, unlike in molten or dissolved states.

quiz.question: Which type of bond involves the transfer of electrons between a metal and a non-metal?
quiz.explanation: Ionic bonds form through electron transfer, typically between a metal (which loses electrons) and a non-metal (which gains them).

quiz.question: Why do metals conduct electricity well?
options: They contain delocalized electrons free to move
quiz.explanation: Metallic bonding involves delocalized electrons that move freely through the metal lattice, enabling electrical conductivity.

quiz.question: What determines whether a bond is ionic or covalent?
quiz.explanation: A large electronegativity difference favors ionic bonding (electron transfer), while a small difference favors covalent bonding (electron sharing).
